notes.meaning: God tells Moses to send three kinds of people out of the camp. These are people with a skin disease, people with a bodily discharge, and anyone who touched a dead body. Some of these were health matters, but the list also includes people who were only "unclean" by the law's rules. "Unclean" here means not fit to come near God in worship. So the main point is keeping God's home pure, not only stopping illness.

The rule is the same for men and women. The reason is that God lives in the middle of the camp, and His dwelling must not be made unclean. Matthew Henry says a church must guard its purity as carefully as its peace. Many older writers also saw this as a picture of a church lovingly setting apart people who openly refuse to turn from sin, until they repent.

The people obeyed right away, just as God had told Moses. Even later in Canaan, people with the skin disease lived outside the towns. Adam Clarke believes those sent out were still treated kindly. He adds that people put out of a church should also be cared for, because they may yet come back.

God gives a new rule about wronging another person, such as cheating or stealing. Hurting a neighbor is also called being unfaithful to the LORD, because God commands us to treat others fairly. "Guilty" here means the person's conscience now troubles them. Calvin notes this is about hidden wrongs that no court may ever find out.

The wrongdoer must admit the sin openly, to God and to the person hurt. Then they must pay back everything, plus one-fifth more. The extra fifth makes up for the loss and also warns others not to do the same. Matthew Henry says that as long as someone keeps what they got wrongly, the guilt stays, no matter how much they pray.

Sometimes the wronged person has died and has no close relative to receive the payment. Then the payment goes to the LORD through the priest. It comes along with a ram offered for atonement, which means making peace with God for the sin. So a person can never use a missing owner as an excuse to keep stolen things. Calvin adds that this stopped people from robbing the dead.

Holy gifts brought to the priest, like the first part of a harvest, belong to him. These are gifts set apart for God, not the parts burned on the altar. Calvin links this to Paul's teaching that those who serve at the altar should live from the altar (1 Corinthians 9:13).

A person may decide what to give. But once a gift is handed to the priest, it is his for good. Matthew Henry says givers could not take a gift back later in a bad mood. He also says it went to the priest who was serving at the time.

God now gives a law for when a husband thinks his wife has been unfaithful. Adultery is treated as a very serious sin, because it breaks the marriage promise. The law had two aims. It warned wives against unfaithfulness, and it shielded wives from angry husbands acting on mere suspicion. Calvin says it shows God Himself guards faithfulness in marriage.

The case is one where nothing can be proved. No one saw anything, and she was not caught. If adultery was proved, the law gave a different and harsher penalty (Leviticus 20:10). This test was only for uncertain cases. Matthew Henry notes that sin tries to hide because it is shameful.

The husband becomes jealous, and the law openly says his wife may be innocent. Calvin says priests should not accept every small or unfair complaint. Matthew Henry gives advice to both sides. Wives should avoid even the look of wrong, and husbands should not hold onto suspicions without cause, since love "thinks no evil."

The husband brings his wife to the priest with a plain offering of barley flour. Usually oil, a sign of joy, and frankincense, a sign of God's welcome, were added. Here they are left out because it is a sad day, and she comes as someone under suspicion. The offering "reminds" of sin and is a serious appeal to God, who knows everything.
The priest brings the woman forward to stand "before the LORD." That means in front of the sanctuary, where the ark of God was kept. The matter is placed in God's hands.

The priest puts holy water in a plain clay jar. Many say the water came from the basin where priests washed. Calvin and the Geneva Notes suggest it may be the special water for cleansing. Dust from the tabernacle floor is added as a sign of lowness and shame. Because it was holy dust, it would make a guilty person more afraid.

The priest lets down the woman's hair and puts the grain offering in her hands, while he holds the bitter water. Some say loosened hair showed sorrow, or that she had lost her husband's protection. Calvin disagrees that it was meant to shame her, since she had not been judged yet. He says it was meant to make her take the moment seriously. Wesley adds that the water had no power of its own; only God could make it work.

The priest puts her under a solemn oath, a promise made before God. He first tells her that if she is innocent, the water will not hurt her. Matthew Henry says no one needs to fear the law's curse who has not broken the law.

Then the priest speaks the other side. If she is guilty, may God make her an example of a curse among her people. "Thigh" is a polite word for the private parts. Her body would waste away, and she would be unable to have children. The Geneva Notes say the curse fit both her sin and her lying under oath.

The woman answers, "Amen, Amen," which means "So be it." Saying it twice showed she was willing for God to deal with her as she deserved. Matthew Henry says a guilty woman could only say this if she did not believe God or was daring Him.

The priest writes the curses on a scroll and washes the ink into the water. In this way she would drink the very words. If she was innocent, it pictured her curse being wiped away, like God blotting out sin (Isaiah 43:25). If she was guilty, the curse would go inside her with the water.
She drinks the water. It is called "bitter" mainly because of what it would bring on a guilty person. Matthew Henry draws a lesson: stolen pleasures may taste sweet, but sin turns bitter in the end.

The priest takes the grain offering from her hands, lifts it before the LORD, and brings it to the altar. Placing an offering in the middle of the test showed that the whole thing was an appeal to God, from whom nothing is hidden.
A handful of the grain is burned on the altar as a "memorial," calling on God to remember and judge. Matthew Henry says the rest was eaten by the priest. After this, the woman drinks the water.

If she is guilty, the curse comes true, and she becomes an example among her people. Water and dust have no natural power to do this. God Himself would act through the test He had set up. Calvin says this was no empty threat. Adam Clarke notes that Scripture records no case of the test being used, perhaps because the guilty were too afraid to try it.

If she is innocent, she is not harmed and will be able to have children. Calvin says this blessing was like God's seal that she was cleared. Matthew Henry takes comfort here: God will find a way to show that the innocent are innocent.

These verses sum up the "law of jealousy." It was not a normal court trial. It was a test that put the matter directly before God. Some think God took a test common in the ancient world and cleaned it of idol worship. Matthew Henry draws a lesson: secret sins are known to God, and one day He will judge them through Christ (Romans 2:16).

The husband is not to blame for bringing the case, even if his wife turns out to be innocent. If she is guilty, she bears the punishment for her own sin. Matthew Henry says we no longer have this water test, but God's Word still warns that He will judge unfaithfulness in marriage.
